items.prompt: What is the name of the chemical reaction that makes a fungus glow?

options.label: Bioluminescence
options.feedback: Correct. Bioluminescence is the production of light by a living organism, and the glow of fungi is one example of it.

options.label: Photosynthesis
options.feedback: Photosynthesis is how plants make food from sunlight, not how fungi produce light.

options.label: Fermentation
options.feedback: Fermentation is a way some organisms break down food without oxygen, and it does not produce light.

options.label: Respiration
options.feedback: Respiration is how cells release energy from food, and while it powers many processes, it is not the name for light production.

items.ok_line: Fungi glow through bioluminescence, the same process seen in fireflies.
items.ko_line: That is a different biological process, not light production.
items.exp_text: Bioluminescence is the production of light by living things. In glowing fungi, a chemical called luciferin reacts with oxygen, and an enzyme called luciferase speeds up the reaction, giving off light. This is the same kind of process that makes fireflies glow, though the chemicals differ slightly.

items.prompt: Which part of a glowing fungus actually gives off the light?

options.label: The cap only
options.feedback: The cap is not the only part that glows. In many species the whole fruiting body can glow, and sometimes the mycelium glows even more brightly.

options.label: The fruiting body and the mycelium
options.feedback: Correct. Both the mushroom (the fruiting body) and the thread-like network called the mycelium can produce light, though in some species only one of them does.

options.label: The spores only
options.feedback: Spores are the tiny reproductive cells, and they do not glow. The light comes from the living tissue of the fungus itself.

options.label: The stem only
options.feedback: The stem is not the only glowing part. Many fungi glow across the whole fruiting body, and the mycelium often glows as well.

items.ok_line: Glowing fungi shine from the fruiting body and the mycelium.
items.ko_line: The light is not limited to a single structure.
items.exp_text: A fungus has two main parts: the visible fruiting body (the mushroom) and the hidden network of threads called the mycelium. Both can be bioluminescent. In some species the mycelium glows continuously, while the mushroom glows only when it is young or fresh.

items.prompt: About how many species of fungi are known to glow?

options.label: About 10
options.feedback: That is far too low. Glowing fungi are not that rare; we know of many more species than ten.

options.label: About 50
options.feedback: That underestimates the number. Scientists have documented many more glowing fungus species than fifty.

options.label: About 150
options.feedback: That is close but still too low. The known count is higher than one hundred and fifty.

options.label: About 100
options.feedback: Correct. Roughly one hundred species of fungi are known to be bioluminescent, spread across different groups.

items.ok_line: Roughly 100 fungus species are known to glow.
items.ko_line: The known number is around one hundred, not less.
items.exp_text: Scientists have identified about one hundred species of fungi that produce their own light. They belong to several different families, and they grow mostly on decaying wood in forests. More species may still be discovered, especially in tropical regions.

items.prompt: Which mushroom is well known for its bright green glow?

options.label: The jack-o'-lantern mushroom
options.feedback: Correct. The jack-o'-lantern mushroom (Omphalotus olearius) glows a bright greenish-yellow, and it is one of the most famous glowing fungi.

options.label: The death cap mushroom
options.feedback: The death cap is a poisonous mushroom, but it does not glow. It is not a bioluminescent species.

options.label: The shiitake mushroom
options.feedback: Shiitake is an edible mushroom grown for food, and it does not glow at all.

options.label: The morel mushroom
options.feedback: Morels are edible spring mushrooms with a honeycomb cap, and they do not produce light.

items.ok_line: This mushroom is famous for its greenish glow.
items.ko_line: That mushroom is not known to produce light.
items.exp_text: The jack-o'-lantern mushroom grows in clusters on dead wood. Its gills and sometimes its whole fruiting body glow with a greenish-yellow light that can be quite striking in the dark. It is one of the most commonly remembered examples of a glowing fungus.

items.prompt: What colour is the light produced by glowing fungi?

options.label: Red
options.feedback: Red light is not produced by fungi. Their glow is in the green part of the spectrum, not the red.

options.label: Blue
options.feedback: Many ocean creatures glow blue, but fungi are different. Their light is greenish, not blue.

options.label: Green
options.feedback: Correct. Nearly all glowing fungi emit green light, usually with a slight yellow or blue tint.

options.label: Orange
options.feedback: Orange is not the typical colour. The glow of fungi is green, not orange.

items.ok_line: Glowing fungi shine with green light.
items.ko_line: Fungi do not glow red, blue, or orange.
items.exp_text: The light from bioluminescent fungi is green, although the exact shade can vary from yellowish-green to bluish-green. This is the same colour range seen in many other land organisms, and it is different from the blue light that dominates the ocean.

items.prompt: What is the leading explanation for why fungi glow?

options.label: To attract mates
options.feedback: Fungi do not mate by flashing light like fireflies do. Their glow serves a different purpose.

options.label: To attract insects that spread spores
options.feedback: Correct. The leading idea is that the glow attracts night-active insects, which land on the fungus and carry away its spores.

options.label: To scare away predators
options.feedback: There is no evidence that the glow warns or scares animals. It is thought to attract, not repel.

options.label: To warm up the surrounding wood
options.feedback: The glow gives off almost no heat, so it cannot warm anything. It is a chemical light, not a thermal one.

items.ok_line: The glow likely attracts insects that help spread spores.
items.ko_line: Mating, warning, and heating are not supported explanations.
items.exp_text: The most widely accepted explanation is that the green light attracts insects, such as beetles and flies, that come to the fungus at night. As they crawl over the fruiting body, they pick up spores and carry them to new places, helping the fungus spread. This idea fits with the fact that the glow is brightest when the fungus is ready to release spores.

items.prompt: Why does glowing wood give off no heat?

options.label: Because the reaction is too slow
options.feedback: The speed of the reaction is not the reason. Even though it is slow, it still makes light without heat.

options.label: Because the wood is wet
options.feedback: Moisture affects whether fungi can grow, but it is not why the glow is cold.

options.label: Because the light is reflected from the moon
options.feedback: The light is not reflected moonlight. It is produced by the fungus itself, and it is cold because of the chemistry.

options.label: Because almost all the energy becomes light, not heat
options.feedback: Correct. In bioluminescence, the chemical reaction converts nearly all its energy into light, so very little is lost as heat.

items.ko_line: Slow speed, wetness, and moonlight are not the explanation.
items.exp_text: In ordinary light bulbs, most energy becomes heat and only a little becomes light. In bioluminescence, the reaction is highly efficient: almost all the chemical energy goes directly into making light, so the glowing wood stays cool. This is why bioluminescence is sometimes called 'cold light'.

items.prompt: What does a glowing fungus feed on?

options.label: Decaying wood
options.feedback: Correct. Most glowing fungi are saprotrophs that break down dead wood and other plant material for food.

options.label: Living leaves
options.feedback: Glowing fungi do not feed on living leaves. They grow on dead organic matter, mainly wood.

options.label: Insects
options.feedback: Fungi do not catch or eat insects. Some carnivorous plants do, but fungi are decomposers.

options.label: Soil minerals
options.feedback: Fungi absorb nutrients from their surroundings, but their main food source is the organic matter they decompose, not plain minerals.

items.ok_line: Glowing fungi feed on dead wood.
items.ko_line: They do not eat living plants, insects, or minerals.
items.exp_text: Most bioluminescent fungi are wood-decaying fungi. Their mycelium grows inside dead trees, branches, and logs, releasing enzymes that break down the tough material. They absorb the nutrients released from the wood, and in the process they help recycle it back into the forest soil.

items.prompt: Why is a glowing fungus so hard to notice on an ordinary walk?

options.label: Because it only glows for a few seconds
options.feedback: The glow is not a quick flash. It is steady, but it is still easy to miss for other reasons.

options.label: Because it is buried underground
options.feedback: The fruiting body grows above ground, though the mycelium is in the wood. The difficulty is not that it is hidden underground.

options.label: Because its light is too dim to see in daylight
options.feedback: Correct. The glow is faint, and during the day sunlight washes it out completely. You can only see it in darkness, after your eyes adjust.

options.label: Because it only glows in winter
options.feedback: Glowing fungi are most visible in warm, wet seasons, not winter, but the real reason is the faintness of the light.

items.ok_line: The glow is faint and invisible in sunlight.
items.ko_line: It is not a quick flash, underground growth, or winter timing.
items.exp_text: Bioluminescent fungi produce only a faint green glow. In the bright light of day, the glow is completely lost. Even at night, it can take several minutes in darkness for your eyes to become sensitive enough to see it. That is why people rarely notice glowing wood on a casual walk, especially during the day.

items.prompt: What is the glow of certain fungi in a wood at night called?

options.label: A firefly flash
options.feedback: Firefly flashes come from insects, not from the wood. The glow on wood has its own name.

options.label: Foxfire
options.feedback: Correct. The steady glow of decaying wood, caused by bioluminescent fungi, is traditionally called foxfire.

options.label: A milky sea
options.feedback: A milky sea is a glow on the ocean surface, caused by bacteria, not a glow on forest wood.

options.label: A red tide
options.feedback: A red tide is a bloom of plankton in the sea, not a glow from fungi on land.

items.ok_line: The glow on wood is called foxfire.
items.ko_line: Those names apply to different bioluminescent phenomena.
items.exp_text: When decaying wood glows in the dark because of fungi, people have long called it foxfire or fairy fire. The name has been used for centuries to describe the soft, eerie light that appears on old logs and stumps in forests at night.
